---
title: "Using AI in Academic Writing"
description: "How to use AI tools carefully in literature searches, drafting, and self-review. What the group requires when you do: citation folders, disclosure, and a usage log."
categories: [Policies, Writing, AI]

## Why this policy exists

AI tools can be a real help in academic writing. They can speed up literature searches, help you
triage a stack of papers, and give you honest feedback on a draft before anyone else sees it. They
can also produce confident, elegant text that is wrong, cite papers that don't exist, and quietly
replace your thinking with theirs. Both of these are showing up in the work I receive, so it's worth
being explicit about what good use looks like.

This is not an AI ban. Personally, I use AI in a lot of my work and I find it effective for many 
different tasks. My goal with this policy is to make sure AI is used carefully and thoughtfully, 
and that the work you put forward is still yours.

The underlying principle is simple: **you must own the work and be able to defend it.** Every
claim, every sentence, and every citation. If you can't explain why something is in your paper,
where it came from, and why you believe it, then it isn't really your work yet. Keep working on it
until you can defend it fully and are confident in what you are putting forward.

Two things make this especially important for trainees:

- **My name goes on the work too.** Before anything is submitted with my name on it, I need to be
  able to do my own due diligence. The requirements below are designed to make that possible.
- **Writing is a skill you build by doing it.** If AI does the writing, you don't learn to write.
  An early study from MIT[^brain] found that people who wrote essays with an AI assistant showed
  lower cognitive engagement, and most of them couldn't quote a passage from the essay they had
  just "written". It's a small study and its conclusions have been debated, but the direction
  matches what I see. By handing off the work of writing means you don't get better at it.

[^brain]: Kosmyna et al., "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI
    Assistant for Essay Writing Task," 2025. [arXiv:2506.08872](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872).

## Guiding principles

1. **You are accountable for everything.** Journals, funders, and the university all agree that AI
   cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility for the work. That responsibility
   is yours.
2. **AI supports your thinking; it doesn't replace it.** Use it to search, sort, question and
   polish. The ideas, the argument and the judgement have to come from you.
3. **Be transparent.** Tell me how you used AI, keep a record, and disclose it wherever it's
   required.
4. **Protect what isn't yours to share.** Unpublished results, other people's manuscripts, and
   potentially patentable ideas need to stay out of places where they could leak.

## Where AI is most useful

### Writing database search queries

Building a good search string for scholarly databases like Scopus and Web of Science, is
tedious: you need synonyms, alternative spellings, Boolean logic, and the right field codes for
each database. AI is very good at this. Describe what you're looking for and ask for a query you
can paste in, then refine it based on what comes back.

```text
I'm doing a literature search on [topic] for [purpose, e.g. a thesis chapter on ...].
I'm particularly interested in [specific aspects], and I want to exclude [things that
are out of scope].

Write a search query for [Scopus / Web of Science / ...] using that database's syntax.
Include common synonyms and alternative terms, and explain each part of the query so I
can adjust it.
```

You still decide which results are relevant. The AI is building the net, not choosing the fish.

### Triaging articles before you read them in full

A short summary can help you decide which papers deserve a full read. This works much better if
you tell the model **what you're looking for**, so it pulls out what's relevant to you instead of
giving a generic summary of the abstract.

```text
I'm attaching a paper. I'm deciding whether to read it in full for a literature review on
[topic]. Specifically, I care about:

- [e.g. which turbulence models were used and how they were validated]
- [e.g. whether they report mesh sensitivity results]
- [e.g. operating conditions or geometry comparable to ...]

In under 200 words, tell me what the paper does, then answer each point above. For each
answer, say where in the paper you found it (section or page). If the paper doesn't
address a point, say so rather than guessing.
```

Asking for locations in the paper lets you check the summary quickly, and asking the model to say
when something isn't addressed discourages it from filling gaps with plausible-sounding guesses. A
summary is a filter, not a substitute: anything you cite, you need to have read.

### Reviewing your own draft

In my experience, this is the most valuable use of AI in writing: as a reviewer, not a writer.

**Language and flow.** AI is good at catching grammar problems, awkward sentences, inconsistent
terminology, and paragraphs that don't connect. Ask it to *point out* problems and explain them,
rather than silently rewriting your text, so you stay in control of the changes and learn from
them.

**Mock peer review.** Before a paper goes to me (or to a journal), have the AI review it from
three different perspectives:

1. An expert in the **exact field** of the work.
2. An expert in an **adjacent field**.
3. A researcher in the **same broad field** with no expertise in your specific topic.

You must name the actual fields in the prompt. "An expert in the field" gives vague feedback;
"an expert in large-eddy simulation of turbulent combustion" gives useful feedback.

```text
I'm attaching a draft manuscript I intend to submit to [journal]. Please review it as three
separate peer reviewers, each writing an independent report:

- Reviewer 1: an expert in [exact field, e.g. immersed boundary methods for fluid-structure
  interaction].
- Reviewer 2: an expert in [adjacent field, e.g. experimental biomechanics of heart valves].
- Reviewer 3: a researcher in [broad field, e.g. computational fluid dynamics] with no
  specific expertise in this topic.

For each reviewer, give a short summary of the paper, the major concerns, minor comments,
and a recommendation (accept, minor revision, major revision, reject). Focus on gaps in the
argument, missing comparisons or validation, unclear explanations, and claims that are not
supported by the results. Be critical; do not soften the feedback.
```

Then treat the output like a real round of peer review. Go through each comment, decide whether
it's valid, and revise the paper as you normally would. Not every comment will be right, and
you should be able to explain why you rejected the ones you did. I've found this reliably
surfaces gaps I hadn't thought about and highlights sections that are unclear to anyone who isn't
as deeply involved in the work as I am.

Only do this with **your own** work. Using AI to review a manuscript or proposal you've been sent
as a reviewer is a different matter; see [Confidentiality](#sec-confidentiality).

## Where to be careful

### References and literature reviews

**Never let AI generate references.** AI models are well documented to fabricate citations. Studies
of ChatGPT-generated references have found that a large share don't exist at all, and many of the
rest have the wrong authors, year, or details.[^refs] The fabricated ones look entirely convincing:
real author names, real journals, and correctly formatted DOIs.

[^refs]: For example, Walters and Wilder, "Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations
    generated by ChatGPT," *Scientific Reports* 13, 14045 (2023),
    [doi:10.1038/s41598-023-41032-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-41032-5); and Bhattacharyya
    et al., "High Rates of Fabricated and Inaccurate References in ChatGPT-Generated Medical
    Content," *Cureus* 15, e39238 (2023),
    [doi:10.7759/cureus.39238](https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.39238). Newer models do better, but
    none are reliable enough to trust without checking.

The rule for the group:

- AI may **suggest** articles you should look at. Treat these as leads, not citations.
- AI must **not cite anything** in your writing unless you have explicitly approved it.
- Before anything is cited, **find the real full-text PDF** yourself and read at least the key
  sections relevant to how you are intending to cite it.
- If you want AI to help with a section that draws on the literature, **give it the real PDFs**
  and tell it to work only from those files. This is the most effective way to keep invented
  references out of your work.

This also feeds directly into the [citation folder requirement](#sec-requirements) below.

### Drafting text

AI is of limited use for writing the prose itself, unless you give very specific instructions about
what you want for a particular section. You need to drive this process if you are going to call it
your own work.

- **Don't ask AI to write a whole document from scratch in one go.** What comes back will be
  generic, will reflect the model's ideas rather than yours, and will be very hard to review
  properly.
- **Start with an outline.** An outline is a reasonable thing to ask AI to help with. Then review
  it critically and edit it until it reflects the argument *you* want to make: reorder it, cut
  things, add what's missing.
- **If AI drafts a section, edit it thoroughly and question everything.** Is this claim true? Is it
  supported by a source? Ask the model where each claim comes from, then check the source yourself.
  Assume anything you can't verify is wrong.
- **Ask whether it says what you mean.** For each paragraph, ask yourself whether it accurately
  represents your ideas and your results. If it doesn't, rewrite it in your own words. Something that
  reads well is not the same as it being correct. Polished text that says something slightly different 
  from what you meant is worse than rough text that says exactly what you meant.

A useful test: could you defend every sentence in front of your committee without looking at your
notes? If not, you're not ready to call this your own work.

### Confidentiality and data training {#sec-confidentiality}

Anything you paste or upload into an AI tool leaves your control. Two things follow from that.

**Turn off training on your data.** Many AI services, especially free personal accounts, can use
your conversations to train future models. Unpublished results, draft papers, and new ideas could
then be exposed. That can compromise a paper, and for anything potentially patentable, it can
compromise the patent. Check the privacy or data settings on every AI account you use and make 
sure model training on your data is **off**. If a service doesn't let you turn it off, don't use 
it for your research work.

**Don't upload other people's confidential material.** Manuscripts you've been asked to review,
grant proposals you're evaluating, and collaborators' unpublished work are not yours to share.
Publishers and the federal funding agencies explicitly prohibit reviewers from putting this
material into AI tools.[^review] The same applies to anything covered by an industry or
collaboration agreement.

[^review]: See, for example, COPE's position on AI and the Tri-Agency
    [guidance on the use of AI in developing and reviewing research proposals](https://science.gc.ca/site/science/en/interagency-research-funding/policies-and-guidelines/guidance-use-artificial-intelligence-development-and-review-research-grant-proposals).

## Recommended tool

The group has a Claude subscription, and **that's what I recommend you use for your research work.** 
It gives you a paid-level account at no cost to you, which matters for the workflows on this page:
uploading full-text papers, long drafts, and sets of PDFs is often not practical on a free personal
account. It also keeps group work under one set of data and privacy settings. If you need access,
ask me.

You're not required to use it, but if you use something else, the same rules apply. Check the data
training settings, and record what you used.

## Group requirements {#sec-requirements}

These apply to any written work you give me: papers, thesis chapters, conference abstracts,
proposals, and reports.

1. **Citation folder.** Submit a shared folder containing the full-text PDF of every article you
   cite. This lets me do my own due diligence before anything goes out with my name on it. If you
   can't find a PDF for something you've cited, that's a sign you should check whether you've
   really read it. If you are citing a physical book, you do not have to obtain a PDF, but you
   must attest that you've actually read the relevant sections of the book that you are citing. 
2. **Disclose your AI use to me.** When you hand in written work, tell me at a high level which AI
   tools you used and what you used them for.
3. **Keep a usage log.** Keep a record of the models you've used (name and version) and how you
   used them. This doesn't need to be a daily session log; it's a high-level record so we can
   write an accurate disclosure later. A suggested format is below, and you can adapt it to your
   needs.
4. **Disclose externally when required.** Journals, conferences, funders, and the graduate school
   increasingly require AI use to be disclosed, and their rules differ (some want a separate
   declaration section, some want it in the methods, some exempt basic copy-editing). Check the
   requirements for wherever the work is going. Your usage log makes this straightforward. Western's
   graduate studies guidance also expects you to discuss AI use in your research with your
   supervisor and committee.[^western]
5. **Protect confidential information.** Follow the [confidentiality](#sec-confidentiality) rules
   above.

[^western]: Western University School of Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies,
    [Guidance for the use of Generative AI in Graduate Studies](https://grad.uwo.ca/about_us/policies_procedures_regulations/ai.html).

### Suggested usage log

Keep one log per piece of work (for example, a text file or table alongside the manuscript or in
the citation folder). One row per *kind* of use is enough; you don't need an entry every time you
open a chat.

| Tool and model version | Used for | Parts of the work affected | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Building Scopus search queries | Literature review | Refined manually; results screened myself |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Targeted summaries to triage ~40 papers | Literature review | Every cited paper read in full |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | Grammar and flow review | Whole manuscript | Suggestions accepted or rejected individually |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Three-persona mock peer review | Whole manuscript | Revised sections 3 and 5 in response |

Record the model name and version as the tool reports it, since journals increasingly ask for
this.

## Quick reference

| Good uses | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Writing and refining database search queries | Letting AI generate or insert citations |
| Targeted summaries to decide what to read | Citing a paper you've only read a summary of |
| Getting help with an outline, then revising it yourself | Asking for a whole document in one go |
| Working from real PDFs you've provided | Trusting claims you haven't checked against a source |
| Grammar, clarity and flow review | Accepting rewrites that don't say what you mean |
| Mock peer review of your own draft | Uploading manuscripts or proposals you're reviewing for someone else |
| Using the group account with training off | Using accounts that train on your data |
